transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I keep getting stuck redoing the same checks and routines over and over at work, even when I know they’re unnecessary, and it’s starting to derail my projects and my life. It has gotten to the point where I just can't seem to stop myself, and I really need some help to figure out why this is happening.
Do you also experience repetitive thoughts or urges that are disturbing or intrusive, in addition to these compulsive behaviors of redoing checks and routines?

Yes, I get these looping, irrational thoughts that if I've missed even a tiny detail, like a mislabeled bolt size, something catastrophic will happen. I keep getting these vivid, disturbing mental images of parts failing and people getting hurt because of my oversight, and I just can't seem to shut them out.

Do these repetitive thoughts or urges to redo checks and routines primarily focus on symmetry, exactness, or avoiding harm to yourself or others, or are they more about contamination, losing control, or making mistakes that lead to severe consequences?

It’s definitely about making a mistake that could lead to severe consequences, rather than symmetry or contamination. I’m consumed by this intense fear that a tiny oversight on my part will cause a catastrophic failure where people actually get hurt. It is the dread of causing that kind of harm through an error that completely drives my checking.

Do you experience any significant anxiety or distress when you're prevented from performing these checking rituals or when you try to ignore these intrusive thoughts about potential catastrophic failures?

Yes, trying to ignore the thoughts causes intense anxiety because those images of parts failing and people getting hurt just loop uncontrollably in my head. I can't shake the nagging feeling that I've missed something, which makes me feel completely chained to my desk. It feels virtually impossible to move on or leave until I actually perform the checks.
Have you started avoiding certain tasks or situations at work or in your daily life because of the fear of making a mistake that could lead to severe consequences?

I don't actually avoid my work tasks, but rather I get obsessively stuck doing them over and over because I'm so terrified of making a catastrophic mistake. However, I have started skipping my personal life, like workouts, paddleboarding meetups, and a beach clean-up I organized, because I feel completely chained to my desk rechecking my work.

Can you tell me if your repetitive behaviors of checking and rechecking are aimed at preventing a specific, dreaded event, such as the catastrophic failures you mentioned, or are they more about following a set of rules or achieving a sense of completeness or perfection?

My checking is definitely driven by the fear of a specific catastrophic event rather than just following rules. I get trapped in these loops because I'm terrified that a tiny error, like a mislabeled bolt or incorrect tolerance, will cause a part to fail and hurt someone. Even though I know it's irrational and also struggle with a nagging feeling of incompleteness, the core driver is preventing those disastrous consequences.

Can you describe if these catastrophic events you fear, such as parts failing and people getting hurt, are specifically related to your area of work or expertise, or if they are more generalized and could happen in any situation?

Yes, these fears are specifically tied to my engineering work rather than being general worries. I get looping thoughts about very specific technical details in my CAD designs, like a mislabeled bolt size or a tolerance being off by a fraction, leading to mechanical parts failing and people getting hurt.
Do you experience these intrusive thoughts and images of catastrophic failures outside of work as well, or are they primarily triggered by your work-related tasks and responsibilities?

While the thoughts are strictly about my work responsibilities—like design flaws and parts failing—they definitely don't stop when I leave the office. They constantly loop in my head even when I'm at home, which has really started to ruin my sleep and keep me from enjoying my paddleboarding club.

Have you ever experienced any episodes of major depression, such as feeling persistently sad, hopeless, or a lack of interest in activities you once enjoyed, alongside these obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors?

No, I haven't really experienced episodes of persistent sadness or hopelessness. My missing workouts and paddleboarding isn't because I've lost interest in them, but rather because I feel so chained to my checking routines that I simply run out of time.
Can you tell me if there are any specific situations or stimuli that trigger these intrusive thoughts and compulsive checking behaviors, or if they seem to occur randomly throughout your day?

They aren't random at all, but are highly triggered by specific tasks at my desk. Whenever I open a CAD file, draft an email, or review design details like bolt sizes and tolerances, it sets off the thoughts of a failure and the immediate urge to repeatedly recheck.

Have you noticed any situations or tasks outside of your work where you also exhibit similar compulsive checking behaviors or feel the urge to do so, or are these behaviors strictly confined to your work-related activities?

The checking behaviors themselves are strictly confined to my work tasks, like reviewing CAD files, emails, and project plans. However, because these routines consume so much of my time, they severely impact my life outside of work. I've had to miss out on sleep, workouts, and paddleboarding meetups just because I'm stuck at my desk so late.

Can you clarify if your obsessive thoughts about catastrophic failures, such as parts failing and people getting hurt, are exclusively focused on preventing harm to others, or if they also involve fears of harm coming to yourself?

The fears are almost exclusively focused on others, specifically the end-users who will eventually use the equipment and products I design. I don't really worry about harm coming to myself; it's the mental images of parts failing and causing catastrophic accidents that injure other people that I can't seem to shut out.
